rows.his_words: Can I spend more?
rows.plain: “build it, then audit 10 calculations, 10 features, 10 flows, 10 decisions.” The Plan redesign was built and then audited against 49 checks — the audit is part of the work rather than something that happens if there is time.
rows.means: Founder: build it, then audit 10 calculations, 10 features, 10 flows, 10 decisions. BUILT: the typed target end to end (store field, engine, a field to type it in, and our 80%-odds figure offered as a labelled suggestion while theirs is blank); the second dial; the closing sentence that projects rather than promises and explains that growth does almost half the work; three sub-tabs with Goals and Prepare landings; the mortgage-versus-Treasury comparison on Cash flow Debt in both directions; 'Can I spend more?' answering in place in plain English with every stepper position a live run; the Social Security claim row answering in place; and the dated obligation leading the decisions list. AUDITED, 49 CHECKS, and the audit was written to FIND things rather than to pass: calculations were re-derived independently rather than compared to the app's own helpers, features were rendered and driven rather than grepped, flows were walked end to end, and every decision was traced to shipped code rather than to a document. THREE REAL DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED, all on day one — the first screen anyone sees. (1) Three of the seven questions were asked TWICE, because the work added a second component owning the same seven; that is the identical 'one question, one place' defect the founder found in Ray's hero, on another screen. (2) Retire-at and plan-to showed the app's own defaults with nothing saying they were ours — the same class as the target nest egg the app used to derive and label as theirs. (3) '$0' still printed for what counts and for big costs, which reads as 'you have nothing' rather than 'you haven't told us yet'; the brief named this and it was still shipping. One audit check failed for a NON-defect and is recorded as such: the dated withdrawal row was absent at age 72, which is correct because required withdrawals start at 73 — the audit setup was wrong, not the app. Workbook: docs/FCC-core-55-70/build-audit-plan-redesign-2026-08-14.xlsx. All four audits are committed as tests, so they re-run on every change rather than being a one-day exercise.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-14; an audit that only confirms what you believe is not an audit.

rows.plain: “we tell the user we include the mortgage payment for the remaining duration — so we state it rather than asking.” The projection now knows a loan payment STOPS when the loan is paid off, instead of carrying it forever, and the app says so rather than asking you to work it out.
rows.means: Founder: we tell the user we include the mortgage payment for the remaining duration — so we state it rather than asking. BUILT, all five pieces. (1) THE SIMULATION NOW KNOWS A PAYMENT STOPS. It charged a person's whole spending figure, inflated, for every year to the horizon — so anyone whose answer included a mortgage was charged it long after the house was paid off. Pat's clears in 2054 and his plan runs to 2058: four years of a payment that will not exist, making his odds pessimistic with no screen saying so. The payment is charged FLAT and never inflated, which is the reason it is a separate field rather than a spending adjustment: a fixed-rate mortgage is the same dollars in 2054 as today, and inflating it for 28 years would overstate it by more than half. (2) WHAT GOES IN CAN VARY BY YEAR, so paying extra is modelled as money not going into savings while the loan runs AND the whole payment freeing up once it clears — both halves, or it is an argument dressed as a calculation. (3) THE EXTRA PAYMENT PERSISTS; it was a text box that forgot the moment you left the screen, so nothing downstream could price it. (4) THE ODDS EFFECT IS TWO FULL RUNS, never a subtraction — the design's placeholder was 67 minus round(extra/500) times 2, a formula that will happily print a number no simulation produced. (5) THE CONSEQUENCE LINE NOW TRAVELS WITH THE CONTROL, which is the gap my own first build left: I moved the mortgage decision to the debt surface and left the retirement effect behind on Retire, exactly the risk the brief named as the whole reason to be careful about the move. TWO CORRECTIONS FOUND WHILE BUILDING: the payoff year rounded UP, putting a 338-month loan in 2055 when its last payment lands October 2054 — a year of a payment that does not exist, on the one figure a person checks against their own statement. And a contribution change dated after retirement does nothing, because there are no contributions then; a mortgage clearing at 79 stops draining savings rather than starting to top them up. Both now pinned. STILL TO DO before the caption can ship: the spending question must stop asking people to include debt payments, or we charge the mortgage twice.

rows.his_words: Not counting loan or mortgage payments — we add those ourselves, from your loans, for as long as they run.
rows.plain: The spending question now EXCLUDES debt payments. It settles who owns the loan: the app does, taken from the loan record itself, so you never have to remember whether your spending figure already had the mortgage in it.
rows.means: Founder: we tell the user we include the mortgage payment for the remaining duration. That settles who owns the loan — the app does, taken from the loan record itself, so the person never has to remember to include it. IT ALSO CREATES ONE RISK, AND THIS CLOSES IT. The spending question was prefilled from what a person spends now, and what they spend now INCLUDES their mortgage, because it is money leaving their account. With the engine now adding the loan on top, an answer given the old way would charge it twice — on Pat that is $2,400 a month counted double, pushing his odds well below the truth. So the question says what to leave out, at the point of answering: 'Not counting loan or mortgage payments — we add those ourselves, from your loans, for as long as they run.' And when a loan is on file it names it: 'We're including your $2,400/mo mortgage until it's paid off in 2054, from your loan.' The payoff year is computed from the loan's own arithmetic, not typed. THE DIVISION OF LABOUR IS NOW VISIBLE RATHER THAN SOMETHING A PERSON HAS TO WORK OUT, which is the same principle as labelling our assumptions 'ours' and the suggested target 'not yours'. All five pieces of the mortgage work are complete: the question, the engine's ending payment, the year-by-year contributions, the persisted extra payment, and the odds as two real runs. The caption the brief said could not ship is now true. Suite 1778 green, typecheck clean, quality gate passing.

rows.his_words: we should change ETFs to just Funds to include Mutual funds.
rows.plain: “we should change ETFs to just Funds to include Mutual funds.” An ETF is one kind of fund, so someone holding a Vanguard mutual fund was reading a label that did not name what they owned. The class is renamed Stocks / Funds.
rows.means: Founder: "we should change ETFs to just Funds to include Mutual funds." ETFs are one kind of fund, and a person holding a Vanguard mutual fund was reading a label that did not name what they own. WHAT CHANGED: the class label everywhere it is shown — the net-worth grouping and its donut, the Performance composition bar, the add-account flow, the itemize picker, and the glossary card, which now reads 'funds — ETFs and mutual funds — that bundle many stocks together'. WHAT THE RENAME EXPOSED, and this matters more than the word: the label was HARDCODED IN EIGHT PLACES instead of read from the one canonical constant, and had already drifted into THREE forms — 'Stocks / ETFs', 'Stocks & ETFs' and 'Stock / ETF' — all reachable in one session. That is the exact failure the calculation module exists to end. A guard now fails the build if any of the dead forms returns (src/__tests__/class_label_guard.test.ts), and it pins the exceptions so it cannot over-reach. WHAT DELIBERATELY DID NOT CHANGE: real product names ('Vanguard S&P 500 ETF' is what that fund is called); the broker-coverage text, which accurately says an institution shares 'stocks, ETFs and mutual funds'; and the internal key `stocks_etf`, which sits in saved user data — renaming that is a migration, not a sweep, and carries risk with no user benefit. Approved mockups still show the old word and were left alone under the never-overwrite-a-mock rule; new mocks use the new label. 1921 tests green, typecheck clean.

rows.his_words: s against two people
rows.plain:
The whole income surface redesigned. Six decisions:
1. Base pay becomes a full screen with one expandable section per earner — gross, 401(k), employer match, and what actually lands.
2. A 14-month dated table when pay varies, rather than one typical figure.
3. BOTH earners are captured, not one: a household on $84,000 plus $54,000 was being read as $84,000 — one person’s income against two people’s spending.
4. A filing-status question, which had never been asked, so every couple was taxed as a single filer.
5. Bonus and company shares follow the same who-earns pattern.
6. Interest and dividends are worked out from your holdings rather than asked for, and treated as TAXABLE BUT NOT SPENDABLE.
rows.means: Income redesigned end to end: base pay as a full screen with one expandable section per earner (gross, 401(k), employer match, what lands); a 14-month dated pay table when pay varies; both earners captured, not one; a new filing-status question; bonus and stock follow the same who-earns pattern; interest and dividends calculated from holdings rather than asked, and treated as TAXABLE BUT NOT SPENDABLE.
rows.why: The app grossed up a typed take-home figure and taxed it back down, removing the 401(k) twice ($1,467/mo adrift). Nobody had ever set a filing status, so every couple was taxed as a single filer ($328–$866/mo). The household income was one person's against two people's spending. Dividends were counted as money you can spend when they are reinvested ($250/mo). Findings B27, B30–B35.

rows.plain: Your tax band is worked out ONCE, from your total income, and every screen reads that one figure. The base-pay screen does not work out a band of its own — a band is set by everything you are taxed on together, so a screen that sees only your wage would show the wrong one.
rows.means: The tax band is produced ONCE, at total income (MK-CF-F-084 taxable annual → MK-CF-F-090 effective rate). The base-pay screen reads that band; it does not work one out. Both band lines in frame 2a call the same function with different income sets, and the screen says what it counted.
rows.why: A band is set by everything taxed together, not by a wage. The code already put it at total income; a second band inside base pay would have been two producers for one figure — the D2 fault we are removing. rows.plain: Every “today” in the app is the person’s OWN calendar day, not the day in universal time. Converting local midnight to universal time moves the date back a day anywhere east of Greenwich — which made every look-back answer “nothing” on a device set to India time.
rows.means: Every 'today' stamp in src/ now uses MK-ST-F-065 isoLocalDate (or monthKey): 15 production files, 13 test files. New guard src/__tests__/local_day_not_utc.test.ts fails on any new call, with an allowlist for values that are genuinely UTC instants (a market bar timestamp, a provider sync cursor).
rows.why: new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10) reads as today and is not — after about 5pm in California it already says tomorrow. An expense logged on the evening of the 31st was filed in the next month, a balance was stamped with a date the person had not reached, and a funded-this-month flag flipped a day early. It was in 35 places; only two were declared helpers the one-name guard could see, so the new guard checks the CALL rather than the name.

rows.plain: A figure’s identifier is issued once against what the figure IS — its family, the words on the screen, the underlying number — and never changes. Before, a number was its POSITION in a list, so inserting one row silently renumbered every figure after it, and 93 audit findings were keyed to those numbers. A finding would have quietly reattached itself to a different figure.
rows.means: New moneykeel_metric_register.json (211 identifiers). nid() takes a key — family, the words on the screen, the underlying figure — and returns the number issued to it, wherever the row later moves. Seeded from the current build: all 223 metric and input identifiers verified unchanged. Proved by inserting a row at the top of the cash-flow list: zero identifiers moved, and the new row took the next free number.
rows.why: A metric's number was its POSITION in a list — nid() counted up as it walked them — so inserting a row silently renumbered every metric after it in that family. 93 audit findings are keyed to those numbers, as are the founder's typed answers: a finding would have reattached itself to a different figure with nothing to show it had. rows.his_words: effective tax rate % from last year
rows.plain: The tax rate is shown where the money is, and can be corrected there. The rate could previously only be changed on a step inside the guided setup — itself unreachable — so the figure driving every take-home in the app could not be put right where you noticed it was wrong.
rows.means: Approved mock income-v4 (v03 archived), frames 2a and 2a-ii. MK-CF-O-001 basePay now returns takenOut {monthly, share, estimated, saysWhat, shortBy}. The base-pay screen shows what comes out; when it is our estimate it says 'federal income tax only', names the gap in MONEY (about 7.7% of a wage for Social Security and Medicare, plus any state), and offers the field. The onboarding Taxes step asks the SAME question in the SAME words. New rule 8c. 243 suites, 2,455 tests green.
rows.why: The rate could only be changed on the Taxes step inside the guided questionnaire — itself unreachable until 28 August — and it asked for an 'effective tax rate % from last year's return'. That phrase means one thing on a return and another on a payslip: our figure is federal income tax only, about 12 points lower. A person could type 18 against our 9.2 and both be right, and their number drives every take-home figure in the app. FOUNDER RULING: the estimate STAYS federal. Payroll tax applies to wages, and our gross also carries rent, dividends and bonuses — applying 7.65% to that total would be wrong, not merely imprecise. State tax cannot be known without asking. So we work out the one thing we can, say so, and let it be corrected.

rows.his_words: Federal tax bracket
rows.plain: The base-pay card names the federal tax bracket, shows the estimated tax in MONEY rather than as a percentage, and says it assumes the standard deduction. A payslip has dollars on it, not a rate.
rows.means: v05 approved; v04 archived. Base pay (2a-ii): 'Federal tax bracket' named, 'Estimated federal tax — assumes you take the standard deduction' in money not a percentage, the shortfall stated, then one field 'The tax rate you want us to use', with a line saying it drives every tax figure in the app. Summary (5a) is a RECAP: it shows the bracket and the tax at whichever rate is in force, says whose it is — 'your rate, 24% (edit on Your base pay screen)' — and asks nothing. New rules 8d (name the bracket, say what the estimate assumed, never 'effective tax rate') and a recap shows, it does not ask.
rows.why: Research: TurboTax divides total tax by AGI, the textbook definition by taxable income, others by total income — three products, three answers for one return, and TurboTax's own forums carry threads arguing it is wrong. So the phrase is a number a person cannot check. Planning tools (Fidelity, Empower) treat an effective rate as an assumption; paycheck tools (ADP, SmartAsset) never use the phrase and divide ALL withholding by gross. This is a paycheck screen, so it follows the paycheck convention and asks for a payslip figure.

rows.his_words: ll use 24% everywhere your take-home matters — cash flow, budget, what
rows.plain: “We’ll use 24% everywhere your take-home matters — cash flow, budget, what’s left over. One-offs like a Roth conversion still use the tax tables.” The screen promises only what a payslip figure can answer: a rate off a payslip is an AVERAGE, and four places need the rate on your NEXT dollar.
rows.means: 2a-ii: "We'll use 24% everywhere your take-home matters — cash flow, budget, what's left over. One-offs like a Roth conversion still use the tax tables." 5a: "Your 24%, used on every figure built from what lands in your bank." Replaces 'every tax figure in the app' and 'here and everywhere else'.
rows.why: A payslip figure is an AVERAGE rate. Four places need a MARGINAL one — the Roth conversion's tax bill, the Roth-vs-Traditional lean, capital-gains rates, and the tax drag in the retirement odds — because they ask what the NEXT dollar costs. Feeding an average into those is wrong invisibly: someone averaging 24% whose next dollar is taxed at 32% would be told a Roth conversion costs $2,400 when it costs $3,200, and advised to do it on that basis. The screen now promises only the half a payslip figure can answer.

rows.his_words: If someone is not working, how can they contribute to 401K?
rows.plain: The app asks about a 401(k) only where you could legally have one — that means a wage, or self-employment earnings. His challenge: "If someone is not working, how can they contribute to 401K?" They cannot. A pension, Social Security, rent or dividends give nobody the right to contribute, so the question is not asked of someone with no earned income.
rows.means: The 401(k) and employer-match steps now appear ONLY for someone self-employed without a wage — a solo 401(k), with no base-pay screen to hold it. A wage brings the base-pay screen, which carries both. No earned income at all means the question is not asked. Four laws in flow_audit cover wage / self-employment only / no earned income / both.
rows.why: Founder challenge: 'If someone is not working, how can they contribute to 401K?' They cannot. The IRS rule is that contributions come out of COMPENSATION — wages, or self-employment earnings. A pension, Social Security, rent or dividends earn nobody the right to contribute, so the version shipped an hour earlier asked a question whose only valid answer was zero. It was also wrong the other way: keyed on 'employment' alone, it denied the screen to a self-employed person with a real solo 401(k).

rows.plain: Every figure set by law is typed in from the published source. The first run against the real figures found three errors: the IRA limits were a year out of date, the bigger catch-up allowance for ages 60 to 63 was missing entirely in an app built for ages 55 to 70, and four of the required-withdrawal divisors were slightly wrong from being interpolated rather than typed.
rows.means: New src/__tests__/statutory_constants.test.ts: the 2026 bracket tables and deductions, the complete IRS Uniform Lifetime Table (72–120, typed in whole; the interpolation fallback deleted), the SECURE 2.0 start ages, and the SSA claim factors (70% at 62, 124% at 70, FRA 67) — all typed in from the published figures, never from our own constants. IRS_LIMITS corrected: IRA 7,000→7,500, catch-up 1,000→1,100 (the 2025 figures had been carried forward). annual401kLimit now knows the 60–63 super catch-up of 11,250. 249 suites, 2,499 tests green.
rows.why: The founder asked how he can trust the formulas given how many errors his reviews find. The honest answer: stop checking the code against itself. First run against the world found the IRA limits a year stale, the 60–63 super catch-up absent — in an app built for ages 55–70 — and four RMD divisors reading 0.1 low because the table skipped ages and interpolated: a $925 understatement of a legally required withdrawal on $500,000 at age 98.

rows.means: Mock v14 — the window selector, designed. A quiet tray (#EEEEE9, 12-point radius, 3-point inset) holds five segments; the chosen window is lifted onto a white card with a soft shadow and dark-green type, the resting windows are separated by hairline dividers inset from the edges (the dividers beside the chosen card are hidden). rows.his_words: “how can I trust the formulas given how many errors his reviews find?” — stop checking the code against itself. Every statutory constant is typed in from its PUBLISHED source, never from our own constants.
rows.plain: Every figure set by law is typed in from the published source — the IRS or the SSA — and never from our own constants. It came from his question of how he can trust the formulas given how many errors his reviews find; the answer was to stop checking the code against itself. The first run against the published figures found three errors: the IRA limits were a year out of date, the bigger catch-up allowance for ages 60 to 63 was missing entirely in an app built for ages 55 to 70, and four of the required-withdrawal divisors were slightly wrong.

rows.his_words: FOUNDER RULING: the tax estimate STAYS FEDERAL. “Payroll tax applies to wages, and our gross also carries rent, dividends and bonuses — applying 7.65% to that total would be wrong, not merely imprecise. State tax cannot be known without asking. So we work out the one thing we can, say so, and let it be corrected.”
rows.plain:
Our tax estimate covers federal income tax only, and says so on the screen. Three decisions:
1. We do not add payroll tax to it. Payroll tax applies to wages, and our gross figure also holds rent, dividends and bonuses — applying 7.65% to all of that would be wrong, not just rough.
2. We do not guess state tax, because it cannot be known without asking.
3. We work out the one thing we can, name the gap in dollars, and let you correct it.

“Yes, ask User to correct, if not input from user, use the budget.” A mortgage can be entered twice — as the Rent / Mortgage budget line and as a Mortgage debt — and until now the app silently took the budget figure and said nothing. Two decisions:
1. Where the two disagree, the app SAYS SO and asks the person to correct it.
2. Until they answer, the BUDGET figure is the one used — so nothing changes in the arithmetic, only in what the person is told.

rows.his_words: Q52 - use option B
rows.plain:
Noted 2026-10-22, what the screen shows now: his DEC-1669 (2026-10-04, every return time-weighted) replaced this — the money-weighted rate described below no longer stands in, and the window Return it was compared with was removed the same day. Where the Return cannot be measured, the Performance tab and the account page show no percent and a sentence saying why, never another method (MK-PF-M-016, MK-PF-M-017). — TODAY, when money moved in or out in amounts large enough that WHEN it moved would decide the percentage, the Return states nothing and the screen shows the dollar walk alone. That person — someone actively adding money — is the one who most needs a rate and currently never sees one.
HIS RULING: show the exact rate there instead. Where the walk now says there is no percentage, it will read that counting when you added money, the rate was X% a year.
WHY THIS IS SAFE, measured: the two methods are not different answers. The window Return divides the gain once by a straight-line average of the money at work; the money-weighted rate compounds each amount over its own days and solves for the rate. On $100,000 with $10,000 added on 1 July and $118,000 at the end, they give 7.6161% and 7.6341% — 0.018 of a percentage point apart. They can never be far apart, because the window Return REFUSES the moment its straight-line shortcut could be off by more than a percentage point. So this fills the gap it leaves and never contradicts it: one return is visible at a time.
WHERE IT CAME FROM: the figure was built 2026-07-14 as its own card on the old Invest screen, and the Performance design he approved on 2026-09-25 (mock v14) removed that card. The function has been correct and reached by no screen since.
rows.means: Where the window Return declines to state a percentage, the money-weighted rate (MK-PF-F-026) is shown there instead — one return visible at a time.

rows.exceptions: Only where the window Return REFUSES. Where it answers, it is the only return shown — the two agree to about 0.01 of a percentage point, so showing both would be noise, and two returns on one screen is the disagreement he caught on 2026-09-25.

rows.his_words: add it to the cash as losing job does not mean loosing rental income too.
rows.plain: The emergency fund counts rent from a property. Rent keeps arriving when pay stops, so each month it is added to the cash: months = cash ÷ (a month of essentials − the rent).
rows.means: Asked of him on 2026-10-04 while the outside review of MK-NW-O-004 theEmergencyFund was being read with him: a renter who owns a rented-out house. He was offered rent added to the cash, or rent taken off the rental mortgage, and chose the cash. Rent arrives every month, so it is added every month, not once — added once, a year of rent would count as one month of it. The rent is the Income summary’s own Rent row (rent less running costs, less calculated tax when the rate is calculated), so two screens cannot show two rents. Where the rent pays for the whole month there is no count of months, and the screen says the cash is not drawn on.

rows.his_words: All return should be True Weighted Return and not Dietz return.
rows.plain: Every return the app shows is a time-weighted return: split the period at every deposit or withdrawal, take each piece’s growth, multiply the pieces. Money added is never counted as earned.
rows.means: His decision, sent with the outside review of Net worth file 1 (moneykeel_note_to_claude_code_TWR.md, 2026-10-04). Not a Modified Dietz return, not a money-weighted return, not a change in balance. It refuses — no figure — when the start day is not recorded, or when money moved and the value just before it was not recorded; it never falls back to another method. A period that starts with nothing starts at the first deposit. A yearly rate is made only for a period longer than a year: (1 + the return)^(365 ÷ days) − 1. "Return on cost" on one holding is a different question and keeps its own name.

rows.plain: Every change that comes out of the outside review of the calculations counts as a change he has approved, and is treated the way his own feedback is: recorded in the decision log, the Changelog, the standard it belongs to, the master file, the tracker and the drawings, the same day. Post Feedback Sync is the sweep that brings all of those level with the code — not only the folding-in of his feedback files.
rows.means: Said in chat on 2026-10-07, after I had reported twice that "no feedback file of yours was waiting" when he asked for a PFS. His point: files going out of date, two files disagreeing, nobody able to tell the latest version — the mess the one-master rule exists to prevent — happens just as easily from audit changes as from his notes. So the review's changes are his decisions: batch 3 (file 3, 2026-10-07) and batch 4 (file 4, 2026-10-07) are approved by this word, as batches 1 and 2 were by DEC-2484. In the same message he answered the one open question of file 4 with "no": the add-up of what is owned does NOT gain a count of accounts with no value yet. TWO GATES were added the same day so this cannot be held by my attention alone: (1) every function and file a standard names must exist and be live (src/__tests__/guard_standards_name_live_things.test.ts); (2) every decision of his since the one-master rule (2026-09-27) must have its Changelog row, or the build stops (check-changelog-anchored.py).

A $25,000 4.5% Treasury worth $24,200 two days before its coupon now reads 5.69%, not 7.44%.

A CD (its yield is its stated rate), a zero-coupon bond and a matured bond get no estimate; on a coupon day nothing has accrued.

rows.plain: Adding a CD asks once: "Bought from the bank, or through a broker?" A bank CD's yield to maturity is its interest rate ($10,000 at 4.2% → 4.20%), and it has no if-rates-move estimate. A broker CD's yield to maturity is worked out like a bond's, from its face value, interest rate, statement value and maturity date ($10,000 face, 4.2%, worth $9,850, 2 years left → about 5.0%), and it gets the if-rates-move estimate like a bond. Before: every CD showed its interest rate as its yield to maturity — my rule of 2026-10-08, which assumed every CD was bought from a bank at face value.
rows.means: Said in chat on 2026-10-10. He pointed out that a CD bought on the secondary market can yield more or less than its coupon. Narrows DEC-2748f (no rate-move estimate for a CD) to bank CDs.

rows.plain: The time-weighted return counts money that arrives on a day as there for that whole day, and money taken out as gone for that whole day: that day's growth is the evening value ÷ (the previous evening's value + money added − money taken out) − 1. A new account opened with $10,000 and worth $10,050 that evening returned +0.50% that day (+$50); worth $9,800, −2.00% (−$200). Vanguard worth $50,000, $10,000 added in the morning, $60,300 that evening: +0.50% (the $300 was earned on $60,000). Before: the money counted as arriving at the end of the day — the first deposit into a new account could not be measured at all, a value below the money just added was refused as a broken record, and the Vanguard day read +0.60%.
rows.means: Said in chat on 2026-10-11, approving my recommendation after he asked why a $10,000 first deposit worth $10,050 that evening showed no return. A refinement of how DEC-1669's time-weighted return splits at a movement; DEC-1669 stands.

rows.plain: When the daily record does not reach back to the window's first day, the beginning is worked back from today. Wealth generated and the walk are now always shown: each holding with a price history (or a CD's stated rate) gives its gain, and a holding with no price history adds no gain (its value is taken as unchanged). Return is the return of the holdings with a history only: their values now added up ÷ their values at the start added up − 1, each start = value now ÷ (1 + its own return over the window); a holding with no history is left out, not counted at 0%. Below the summary: "Wealth generated and Return do not include Treasury 2031's gains, as it has no price history." Example: an account of $50,000 = VTI $40,000 (+10% over the past year) + Treasury 2031 $10,000 typed by hand, no money moved: VTI gained 40,000 × (1 − 1 ÷ 1.10) = $3,636.36; beginning $46,363.64; Wealth generated $3,636; Return +10.00%. Before: Wealth generated —, Return —, no walk, and "The beginning can't be worked back: Treasury 2031 has no price history."

rows.means: His recommendation, approved in chat on 2026-10-13 with the word "approved." It replaces DEC-3035i (2026-10-07: "Performance draws no walk for a window its record exists but cannot reach; a sentence names the record's first day"). A window whose beginning the daily record cannot read is now worked back by the DEC-3656 / DEC-5068 path whether or not a record exists: beginning = today's value − each holding's known gain − money put in + money taken out; Return = the return of the holdings with a history (knownHoldingsReturn); a holding with no history adds $0 and is named. DEC-3035i's sentence ("The record begins …, so it cannot say what this account was / these accounts were worth on …") still shows, and the window is still greyed, only where NO holding in that window has a history — nothing real to work back from, so a typed value is never carried back to a day nobody recorded (DEC-0230 holds). Cash (uninvested cash, a cash position) gains $0, is not named as "no price history", and is not in Return. A window the record DOES reach keeps the measured time-weighted return (DEC-4439), unchanged. SOME ACCOUNTS REACH, SOME DO NOT: the accounts the record reaches are read and measured together as before (an account with no history that joined the record late still arrives as money put in, DEC-4439); each account it does not reach that has a holding with a history is worked back on its own, exactly as its card is; the summary is these parts added up, so every walk line of the summary equals the same line on those cards added up (an account whose card is greyed adds only its value now). Return there = Σ values now ÷ Σ (value now ÷ (1 + return)) − 1 over the reached accounts together (their measured return) and each worked-back holding with a history. DAY-ONE LINE: where any longer window is worked back, "You added your accounts today. Figures for 1M, 1Y and longer come from each holding's past prices." rows.his_words: two marco points (1) the return listed in the timebar at the top is not accurate for all screens except StateA. (2) Rule is to return % should include price change, dividend and interest, so showing 0% return for bond is not accurate. How about we change the table titles to Market Value / face Value, and Return / YTM as $5000 is face value not market value? Thoughts? ||| approved.
rows.plain: Three parts. (a) A bond's or CD's return over a window is its price change PLUS the interest it was paid in the window: interest and coupon records dated on or after the window's first day that name that holding (or, naming no holding, sit in an account that is that one bond or CD). Return = (1 + price change) × (1 + interest ÷ value today) − 1, which is (value today + interest) ÷ value at the start − 1. KeyBank CD $5,000, price flat, $100 interest → +2.00%; US Treasury $4,000, $85 → +2.125%, shown +2.13%; the Bonds & CDs bar $9,000, $185 → +2.06%. Only an individual bond or CD counts its interest this way (Bonds & CDs, no fund word in its name, not a Treasury-bill ETF, and a CD type, a 9-character security id, a maturity date, a coupon rate or a face value to say it is one instrument); a bond fund's distributions are already in its adjusted closes (DEC-4644), so nothing is counted twice. An account's own time-weighted return (DEC-4439) measures its whole value, the interest that landed in its cash included, and does not change. (b) The columns keep one meaning each (DEC-0093): MARKET VALUE is market value and adds up to the account; RETURN is the window return with interest. The line under a bond's or CD's name shows its face value, coupon rate and yield to maturity, as a stock's shows its shares: $5,000 face · 4.00% · YTM 4.00%. A bank CD's yield to maturity is its rate; a part not given is left out. (c) The account-page drawing's window bar on every state (A to E) is the app's own figure, read off the built screen with each state's data; a window the app greys is a dash, and the grey placeholders are gone.
rows.means: His two points, 2026-10-19, and his word approved on the recommendation. Before: a bond held inside a brokerage showed what its price did and nothing else, so a CD paying 4% read +0.00% (the account-page drawing v01, state A, row 28); and the window bar on states B to E was reasoned, not run. Running the five states through the built screen also found four faults, fixed the same day: (1) the account page used the record's first day as a stand-in purchase date for a holding with no dated lot, so on a record that begins today every worked-back window showed the return on cost (state D 1Y read +25.00% where VTI's prices give +10.00%) — it now asks this account's earliest BUY, the Performance tab's rule; (2) the Since window named the picked window's beginning (state D read Since Sep 29, 2025) — it now names the record's first day, or today; (3) the income line under a holding looked the holding up by its name, so a bond shown by its name matched no record — it now looks up the ticker; (4) a percent exactly on a half (+2.125%) was written +2.12% by the computer's binary rounding — the one percent writer now rounds half away from zero. A coupon record now counts as interest wherever income is added (the ledger already booked it so). The holdings note now says a bond's or CD's interest is added: his DEC-5848 sentence gains that one clause, so it stays true.

rows.his_words: state A - Oct 1, 2025 → Sep 30, 2026 return is 8.26% and 1Y return is 7.12%. Why different as Oct 1 to sept 30 is 1 Year. ||| approved.
rows.plain: Where a window's first day is before the daily record begins, its return is two parts multiplied: the days before the record's first day, worked back from each holding's price history (holdings with a history only, DEC-5068 and DEC-5291; a bond's or CD's interest added, DEC-6212), and the record's own time-weighted return from its first day to today (DEC-4439), the one Since shows. Return = (1 + the days before) × (1 + the record's part) − 1. The walk is joined the same way: its beginning is the record's first value worked back over the days before it (less what the holdings gained then and the money moved then), then the record's walk; it still adds up to today's ending. Only holdings held on the record's first day count in the days before it (one bought later had no part in them); an account the record holds later counts only if the record's part works it back on its own. The left-out sentence is DEC-6076's, said of the days before the record only, and only when those days are worked back: "Before Oct 1, 2025, when the daily record begins: Return is on the $X with a price history. <name> ($Y) has no price history, so its gains are not included." Its amounts are today's values, as DEC-6076 has them: $X = today's value of the holdings the days before count; $Y = today's value of each one left out. Example, the account-page drawing's state A: the record begins Oct 1, 2025; 1Y's beginning is Sep 29, 2025; VOO's price history holds $522.43 on Sep 29 and no close again until Dec 31, so VOO moved 0.00% over those days; the bonds were bought Apr 2, 2026, so they had no part. 1Y = (1 + 0.00%) × (1 + 8.26%) − 1 = +8.26%, the same as Since (was +7.12%); 2Y = (522.43 ÷ 460.00) × 1.0826 − 1 = +22.95%, a year over 731 days +10.87% (was +9.57%). Unchanged: a record that begins today (DEC-5291's answer — state D's 1Y +10.00%), a record that reaches back the whole window (the measured return), and a window whose days before the record cannot be worked back (nothing with a history there: DEC-5291's answer, or its refusal).
rows.means: His question, 2026-10-19, on the account-page drawing's state A, and his word "approved." on the fix: join the two methods instead of choosing one. The cause: 1Y opens one day before the daily record begins, so DEC-5291 switched the whole window to the worked-back-from-prices method (holdings with price history only, weighted by today's values), while Since is the measured time-weighted return of the whole account (DEC-4439). It amends DEC-5291 for a record that exists and begins inside the window; the rest of DEC-5291 stands. The Performance tab's v17 phone 1 moves the same way: 1Y +6.10% → +7.46% (= Since), 2Y +11.10% → +11.81% a year. The note under the summary on the account page and the Performance tab, for such a window: "Your daily record begins Oct 1, 2025, so the days before it are worked back from each holding's price history." rows.his_words: always the class broker sends.
rows.plain: “always the class broker sends.” For a linked or imported holding, the class the broker sends decides what it is. The name, a maturity date and the app's other automatic rules are used only when the broker sends no usable class. A class the person sets themselves still outranks every automatic rule. Example: a money-market fund the broker flags as cash is Cash; a T-bill ETF the broker sends as an ETF is Stocks / Funds.
rows.means: His answer, 2026-10-20, to the question put to him that two of his rulings conflict on which comes first when deciding an asset's class: its name, or the class the broker sends. The two were brief B7 (DEC-0309, 2026-08-20: the name first, the broker's tag only a fallback) and his Q10 answer (DEC-2159, 2026-09-30: the institution's own class field first), which had not been built because it contradicted B7. Before: the person's own class, then the name, then a maturity date, then the broker's cash-equivalent flag, then the broker's type tag. Now: the person's own class, then the class the broker sends (its cash-equivalent flag, else its type), then the name, a maturity date and the other automatic rules. What moves, as shown to him in the worked example: a money-market fund the broker flags is Cash (it was Stocks / Funds by DEC-0051 and DEC-0092); a bond ETF or T-bill ETF the broker sends as an ETF is Stocks / Funds (it was Bonds & CDs by its name and DEC-0051's T-bill rule); an individual bond or CD the broker sends as a bond stays Bonds & CDs.

A value typed today from a statement dated Sep 30 is booked on Sep 30, not today. Example: a Treasury on record at $24,650, retyped on Oct 20 at $24,900 as of Sep 30. rows.means: The Bonds and Other investments editors let a person date a typed value (Value as of). The daily record was written from today's accounts, so the new value read as a change today. Now the save walks back over the days already recorded, from the latest to the as-of date, and puts the new value on each day that still holds the value being replaced; the daily net worth and cash-plus-investments totals move by the same amount on each day moved. Limits: only days already recorded for the account, none invented (DEC-0230); the walk stops at a day holding a different value (a sale, an earlier typed value); a typed balance only, never a linked account or one with holdings; a date that is not a real day, or after today, moves nothing; only a save that states its date moves history.

rows.means: Before 2026-10-21 the sync dropped the broker's minus, so a reversed $500 deposit was saved as $500 put in. The mirror: a broker's +$300 withdrawal is a withdrawal reversed, $300 that came back in. Assumption, noted: SnapTrade sends a withdrawal as a negative amount (the money.ts rule).

rows.plain: NOT A DECISION OF HIS — the lead's decision of 2026-10-21 under his rulings DEC-3523 (tenet 3, unknown is not zero), made without asking him, as his order of 2026-09-30 says. A holding with one purchase dated and another whose date is not on record shows no return since purchase; the card says a purchase has no date on record, so its return since purchase cannot be measured. Its value, what was paid and the gain stand. 7.25 shares dated Sep 17 at $83.17 and 3.125 undated at $91.43, $97.31 today: no return (before: +13.60%, the undated purchase put on the dated day). To reverse: put an undated purchase on the first dated purchase's day again. One word from him reverses it.
rows.means: Before 2026-10-21 returnSincePurchases and earliestPurchaseDate placed a purchase with no date on the dated purchase's day, a guessed day. Now the row carries undatedPurchase, periodReturn and periodTotal are not known, and the Holding page prints the reason where its price-history line would be. The day the holding began is not on record either (MK-PF-F-012).

rows.plain: NOT A DECISION OF HIS — the lead's decision of 2026-10-21 under his rulings DEC-0237 and DEC-3768b, made without asking him, as his order of 2026-09-30 says. Every screen makes a window longer than a year yearly by one rule: (1 + the window's total) to the power 365 ÷ its days, less 1. A window of a year or less, counted on the calendar, is never made yearly. 21% over the 731 days of a 2Y window is +9.99% a year on the Performance tab, the account page and a holding's own page; the holding read +10.00% (exactly two years). Over 2Y the account page says the window's own total and the yearly rate, in the Performance tab's sentence. To reverse: set periodReturnParts back to years = 2. One word from him reverses it.

rows.plain: NOT A DECISION OF HIS — the lead's decision of 2026-10-23 under his rulings DEC-0274 and DEC-4646, made without asking him, as his order of 2026-09-30 says. 1 contract bought at $2.50 costs $250 (cash moved $2.50 and the activity said "1 share"); 1 sold at $3.00 brings in $300, realized +$100, matched first in line to the Aug 3 contract bought at $2.00. The cash, the activity amount and the sheet's cash check all count contracts × the holding's shares per contract × price. Records made before 2026-10-23 stay at ×1, as they were applied. Limit: a ticker bought before it is held counts ×1, because the trade sheet does not ask the holding's type. To reverse: drop the stamp in recordTransaction. One word from him reverses it.

The same-day order in the realized gain (a purchase before a sale) is kept. To reverse: in eventDays, keep each sale on its own day. One word from him reverses it.

rows.plain: NOT A DECISION OF HIS — the lead's decision of 2026-10-24 under his rulings DEC-1923 and DEC-3523 (tenets 1 and 4), made without asking him, as his order of 2026-09-30 says. October's card is unchanged, $1,150. ACTUAL no longer lists the car loan as due the 28th at $0; MONTHLY RECURRING EXPENSES reads $2,400 (it read $2,650); the tax bill is on the BIG-TICKET RADAR at $1,000; Home's due-soon reminder no longer fires for a loan not yet started. MK-CF-M-047, 048 and 049 now say they print on a later month's plan card, from the grid ($7,200 / $6,050 / $1,150), and the retired surplus line and the paycheck card's SURPLUS have their own number, MK-CF-M-078 (it printed under MK-CF-M-049). rows.plain: NOT A DECISION OF HIS — the lead's decision of 2026-10-26 under his rulings DEC-7938 and DEC-3523 (tenet 4), made without asking him, as his order of 2026-09-30 says. Both multiplied the monthly 401(k) by 12, so a July-to-December worker's room was worked on $12,000; it is worked on the $6,000 put in. They read ownK401Annual, one person's 401(k) × their paid months, not MK-CF-F-188, which adds both earners while the limit is per person ($1,200 + $400 would read $19,200 against the person's own $14,400). A full-year earner sees the same figure. To reverse: call householdPreTaxContributionsAnnual there instead. One word from him reverses it.

rows.plain: NOT A DECISION OF HIS — the lead's decision of 2026-10-25 under his rulings DEC-0447, DEC-7940 and DEC-0296, made without asking him, as his order of 2026-09-30 says. A one-time $2,000 with no year counted in 2026 and again in 2028. It counts in no year and reads “year not entered”. rows.plain: NOT A DECISION OF HIS — the lead's decision of 2026-10-25 under his ruling DEC-0641, made without asking him, as his order of 2026-09-30 says. A $9,000 card at 24% with a $200 minimum paid at $300, and a $14,000 car loan at 6.9% at $250, on Oct 1, 2026: the plan ran on the minimums, “$450 /month total”, debt-free Oct 2033, $14,787 of interest. It reads “$550 /month total”, Jun 2031, $7,647. A payment set counts even when no minimum was typed. This replaces the words “This line does not change the payoff plan’s figures” on the 2026-10-25 row about a payment above the minimum. To reverse: pay the minimums. One word from him reverses it.
rows.means: Payments are what actually leaves (DEC-0641), in the plan too.

rows.plain: NOT A DECISION OF HIS — the lead's decision of 2026-10-27 under his ruling DEC-3523 (tenet 1), made without asking him, as his order of 2026-09-30 says. The file and the code disagreed on the senior deduction. The code takes 6% of the income over $150,000 off each person's $6,000 (IRC §151(d)(5)(C)(iii)(I)); the file took it once off the couple's $12,000. Married filing jointly, both 65 or over: $200,000 gives $6,000 and $250,000 gives $0, where the file said $9,000 and $6,000. The IRS says the deduction is gone at $250,000 joint, which only the per-person reading gives. The code was right; the file is fixed. To reverse: put the old entry back in moneykeel_code_formula.py. One word from him reverses it.

A $10,400 CD at 4.00% held beside 100 VTI read ‘KEYBANK CD has no price history’ and the 1Y return was VTI’s alone, +11.11%. Interest paid out is not added on top. To reverse: drop the stated rate inside a brokerage. One word from him reverses it.
